## TL;DR

This is a longer article explaining the workings and the choices behind the GAM nowcasting model and its advantages and limitations.

## Why `nowcasting_mgcv()`

`nowcasting_mgcv()` fits the same nowcasting model as `nowcasting_inla()`, a
negative binomial model for the delay triangle with smooth effects for time and
delay, but as a generalised additive model (GAM) with
[`mgcv`](https://CRAN.R-project.org/package=mgcv) instead of `INLA`. `mgcv` is on
CRAN and is installed together with `nowcaster`, so this function works out of the
box, which makes it a good choice when `INLA` cannot be installed or when a fast
estimate is needed.

## The model

Let $Y_{t,d}$ be the number of cases with onset in week $t$ that were reported
with a delay of $d$ weeks. The model is

$$
Y_{t,d} \sim \text{NegBinom}(\lambda_{t,d}, \phi), \qquad
\log(\lambda_{t,d}) = \alpha + f_1(t) + f_2(d),
$$

where $f_1$ and $f_2$ are penalised thin plate regression splines and $\phi$ is the
dispersion parameter, all estimated by `mgcv::gam()`. The cells of the delay
triangle that are not observed yet ($t + d$ beyond the present week) are then
predicted. The uncertainty is propagated by sampling 1,000 sets of coefficients
from their approximate posterior distribution and, for each set, sampling the
unobserved counts from the negative binomial distribution. Summing the observed and
sampled counts over the delays gives 1,000 trajectories of the epidemic curve, which
are summarised by their median and 50% and 95% intervals.

## Non-structured nowcasting

We use the SARI data from Belo Horizonte shipped with the package. The function
needs the data set and the names of the onset and report date columns.

```{r data}
library(nowcaster)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)

data(sragBH)
```

```{r no-age}
now_mgcv <- nowcasting_mgcv(dataset = sragBH,
                            date_onset = DT_SIN_PRI,
                            date_report = DT_DIGITA,
                            data.by.week = TRUE)
names(now_mgcv)
head(now_mgcv$total)
```

`total` holds the estimate for each week of onset (`dt_event`): the `Median`, the
50% interval (`LIb`, `LSb`) and the 95% interval (`LI`, `LS`). With
`data.by.week = TRUE`, `data` holds the delay triangle used to fit the model, from
which we get the curve as observed at the time of the last record:

```{r observed}
observed <- now_mgcv$data |>
  group_by(dt_event) |>
  summarise(observed = sum(Y, na.rm = TRUE))

ggplot(now_mgcv$total, aes(x = dt_event)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = LI, ymax = LS), fill = "grey70", alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = LIb, ymax = LSb), fill = "grey50", alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_line(aes(y = Median, colour = "Nowcasting")) +
  geom_line(data = observed, aes(y = observed, colour = "Observed")) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(Nowcasting = "black", Observed = "grey50"),
                      name = "") +
  scale_x_date(date_breaks = "2 weeks", date_labels = "%V/%y") +
  labs(x = "Week of onset of symptoms", y = "Number of cases") +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom", axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 90))
```

## Controlling the estimation window

Three arguments, all in weeks, control which part of the data enters the model:

* `Dmax`: the maximum delay considered (default 15). Cases reported later than
  `Dmax` weeks after onset are discarded.
* `wdw`: the length of the window, counted back from the last onset week, used to
  fit the model (default 30).
* `trim.data`: the number of most recent weeks to drop before fitting (default 0).

A shorter window makes the fit faster and more local:

```{r window}
now_short <- nowcasting_mgcv(dataset = sragBH,
                             date_onset = DT_SIN_PRI,
                             date_report = DT_DIGITA,
                             Dmax = 10,
                             wdw = 20)
tail(now_short$total)
```

Keep `Dmax` at 9 weeks or more: the smooth for the delay uses 10 basis
functions and needs at least as many distinct delays.

## Structured nowcasting, by age

Delays differ between age groups, so the model can be fitted with one smooth for
time and one for delay per age class. Pass the age column to `age_col` and choose
the age classes with `bins_age` (`"SI-PNI"`, `"10 years"`, `"5 years"` or a vector of
break points).

`method.group.gam` selects how the smooths are shared between age classes:

* `"fs"` (default): a factor smooth, `s(Time, age_class, bs = "fs")`, where the
  curves of the age classes share one smoothing parameter;
* `"by"`: one independent smooth per age class, `s(Time, by = age_class)`, plus an
  intercept per age class.

```{r age}
now_age <- nowcasting_mgcv(dataset = sragBH,
                           date_onset = DT_SIN_PRI,
                           date_report = DT_DIGITA,
                           age_col = Idade,
                           bins_age = "10 years",
                           method.group.gam = "fs")
names(now_age)
head(now_age$age)
```

The element `age` has the estimate for each age class, while `total` sums the
trajectories over the age classes. The column `fx_etaria` holds the age class
(here "0-9" to "90+") and `fx_etaria.num` its number, in increasing order of age:

```{r age-plot, fig.height=6}
now_age$age |>
  ggplot(aes(x = dt_event, y = Median)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = LI, ymax = LS), fill = "grey70", alpha = 0.6) +
  geom_line() +
  facet_wrap(~fx_etaria, scales = "free_y") +
  labs(x = "Week of onset of symptoms", y = "Number of cases") +
  theme_bw()
```

## Faster fits with `bam()`

The structured model has many more smooth terms, and `mgcv::gam()` can take
close to a minute on these data. The argument `fit` chooses how the model is
fitted:

* `"gam"` (default): `mgcv::gam()`, as above.
* `"bam"`: `mgcv::bam()`, designed for large data sets. It was about 7 times
  faster here, with nowcasts within about 1% of `"gam"`.
* `"bam_discrete"`: `mgcv::bam(discrete = TRUE)`, which also discretises the
  covariates. It was over 40 times faster, but with the factor smooth
  (`method.group.gam = "fs"`) the estimates for the most recent weeks were up to
  about 8% lower than with `"gam"`, still inside its 95% intervals.

```{r fit-options}
now_age_bam <- nowcasting_mgcv(dataset = sragBH,
                               date_onset = DT_SIN_PRI,
                               date_report = DT_DIGITA,
                               age_col = Idade,
                               bins_age = "10 years",
                               fit = "bam")

now_age_bam_discrete <- nowcasting_mgcv(dataset = sragBH,
                                        date_onset = DT_SIN_PRI,
                                        date_report = DT_DIGITA,
                                        age_col = Idade,
                                        bins_age = "10 years",
                                        fit = "bam_discrete")

tibble(dt_event = now_age$total$dt_event,
       gam = now_age$total$Median,
       bam = now_age_bam$total$Median,
       bam_discrete = now_age_bam_discrete$total$Median) |>
  tail(4)
```

The three fits agree on the earlier weeks and differ most in the last ones,
where the nowcast relies most on the model.

## Forecasting

Setting `K` to a positive number adds `K` weeks beyond the last onset week to the
delay triangle, so the model also forecasts cases that have not started yet. Here
we cut the data on 4 July 2020, as if we were nowcasting at that date, and forecast
two weeks ahead:

```{r forecast}
srag_2020 <- sragBH |>
  filter(DT_DIGITA <= as.Date("2020-07-04"))

now_forecast <- nowcasting_mgcv(dataset = srag_2020,
                                date_onset = DT_SIN_PRI,
                                date_report = DT_DIGITA,
                                K = 2)
tail(now_forecast$total, 4)
```

Because the data set holds every case reported up to 2022, we can compare the
estimate with what was eventually observed:

```{r forecast-plot}
eventually_observed <- sragBH |>
  mutate(dt_event = DT_SIN_PRI - as.numeric(format(DT_SIN_PRI, "%w"))) |>
  count(dt_event, name = "observed") |>
  filter(dt_event >= min(now_forecast$total$dt_event),
         dt_event <= max(now_forecast$total$dt_event))

now_forecast$total |>
  mutate(part = ifelse(Time > max(Time) - 2, "Forecasting", "Nowcasting")) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = dt_event)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = LI, ymax = LS, fill = part), alpha = 0.3) +
  geom_line(aes(y = Median, colour = part)) +
  geom_line(data = eventually_observed,
            aes(y = observed, colour = "Eventually observed")) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(Nowcasting = "black", Forecasting = "orange",
                                 `Eventually observed` = "red"), name = "") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(Nowcasting = "grey50", Forecasting = "orange"),
                    guide = "none") +
  scale_x_date(date_breaks = "2 weeks", date_labels = "%V/%y") +
  labs(x = "Week of onset of symptoms", y = "Number of cases") +
  theme_bw() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom", axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 90))
```

The last two weeks are the forecast. Their intervals are much wider, as no case
with onset in those weeks had been observed at the time.

## Trajectories and trend

With `trajectories = TRUE` the function also returns the 1,000 sampled
trajectories. They can be summarised in other ways, for instance to classify the
trend of the curve in the last weeks with `slope.estimate.quant()` (which needs the
`lme4` package). It fits a line to each trajectory over the last `window` weeks and
returns `1` if the curve is increasing, `0.5` if probably increasing, `0` if stable
or uncertain, `-0.5` if probably decreasing and `-1` if decreasing:

```{r trajectories}
now_traj <- nowcasting_mgcv(dataset = srag_2020,
                            date_onset = DT_SIN_PRI,
                            date_report = DT_DIGITA,
                            trajectories = TRUE)
head(now_traj$trajectories)
```

```{r slope, eval=requireNamespace("lme4", quietly = TRUE)}
slope.estimate.quant(trajectories = now_traj$trajectories, window = 3)
```
